options.misconception: Treats a small settler population as a reason to abandon the colony.
options.text: France abandoned New France because it had too few settlers.

options.misconception: Reverses the cause — few settlers meant France needed Native partners more, not less.
options.text: France could ignore Native peoples because it had so few settlers.
France relied on Native partners and allies, since few Frenchmen could work the fur trade.

options.misconception: Mistakes a fur-trading colony for a plantation colony.
options.text: France turned New France into a plantation colony worked by enslaved laborers from Africa.

rationales.A: France kept New France for over a century with few settlers; small numbers shaped its policy, they did not end the colony.
rationales.B: Few settlers meant France needed Native partners more, not less, because Frenchmen alone could not work the fur trade.
rationales.C: With few settlers of its own, France's fur trade depended on Native partners who hunted and carried the furs.
rationales.D: New France stayed a fur-trading colony; its labor system was partnership with Native peoples, not plantation slavery.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the French row. Few settlers, mostly single men, and no exact count — France barely moved people.
2. Ask how a colony with so few people still worked. Background: the fur trade ran through Native partners who knew the woods and rivers.
3. Ask what few settlers force a colony to do. It cannot farm or fight on its own, so it must make friends and trade.
4. Name the pattern. Small numbers made alliance a necessity for France, and the fur trade turned that necessity into a policy.
Remember: when a colony is tiny, ask who does its work, and the answer is usually the people it had to befriend.

stimulus.source_note: Table built from figures given in the three books; France's count is given qualitatively because the books give no exact number.
stimulus.text:
Early Atlantic crossings, 1607-1650

| Group | People | When |
|---|---|---|
| Spaniards to the New World | About 350,000 | By 1650 |
| English settlers at Jamestown | 144 landed; only 38 still alive a year later | 1607-1608 |
| English settlers at Jamestown | About 500 in the colony; nearly 90% died in the 'starving time' | Winter 1609-1610 |
| English settlers to Massachusetts Bay | More than 20,000 | 1630-1642 |
| French settlers to New France | Few, mostly single men; the books give no exact count | 1600s |
